name: South Beach diet

card.summary: A three-phase lower-carbohydrate eating plan favoring lean protein, vegetables and unsaturated fats that people use to lose body fat and look leaner.
card.note: Phase 1 is restrictive; a case report describes ketoacidosis in a person on the diet.

quick.overview:
The South Beach Diet is a modified low-carbohydrate plan created by Miami cardiologist Arthur Agatston in the 1990s. It emphasizes lean meats, vegetables and mostly monounsaturated fats while limiting refined carbohydrates such as white bread, rice and potatoes. People use it to lose body fat, which sharpens facial and physique definition.

It runs in three phases: a strict first phase for fast initial loss, followed by phases that reintroduce whole-grain carbohydrates. Small studies show weight and body-fat reductions in participants with metabolic syndrome, while reviewers have commented on the strength of the book's claims.
quick.how: Followers eat three meals and two snacks a day built around lean protein, vegetables, nuts and healthy oils, avoiding refined carbohydrates in the first phase and gradually adding whole grains later. There is no calorie counting; the plan includes an exercise component. People typically follow it for weeks to months while tracking weight change.
quick.risks: The UK NHS notes phase 1 may cause loss of some vitamins, minerals and fiber, with dizziness and constipation. A published case report describes ketoacidosis in a man three weeks into the diet, and a review of popular plans examined micronutrient adequacy. People with diabetes or other conditions are generally advised to follow medical guidance.

lead: The South Beach Diet is a low-carbohydrate, higher-protein eating plan developed in the mid-1990s by cardiologist Arthur Agatston with dietitian Marie Almon, first as the Modified Carbohydrate Diet for his patients and later renamed for the Miami neighborhood.[1] The first book appeared in April 2003, and about eight million copies were in print by 2004.[1]

For looks, the diet is used as a fat-loss method: lower body fat is associated with more visible jawline and facial definition and a leaner physique.[1] It favors lean meat, vegetables and unsaturated fats, bans refined carbohydrates at first, and does not limit calories or require carbohydrate counting.[1]
Research includes small clinical trials of the commercial plan and several commentaries on the book's nutrition claims.[2][3][4]

chain: Lower refined carbohydrate intake with protein and unsaturated fats
Body weight and body fat fall
Leaner face and more defined physique
angle.text: People use the plan to reduce body fat, which changes how defined the face and physique appear. The diet itself is a nutrition approach, and the look change comes from the weight loss it produces.

paras: The plan has three stages that gradually add carbohydrates while reducing fat and protein; the first targets rapid weight loss and the later two are considered nutritionally adequate.[1] It prefers monounsaturated fats and low-glycemic carbohydrates and recommends three meals plus two snacks a day.[1]

Agatston developed the diet for cardiac patients, a 1999 Miami television segment brought it local fame, and the book followed in 2003.[1] A Supercharged edition came in 2008 and a keto-friendly version was announced in December 2018.[1] Nutrisystem bought the brand in 2015.[1]

In a 12-week study of 20 adults with metabolic syndrome using the commercial plan, body weight fell from 93.5 to 88.3 kg and BMI also decreased, alongside changes in gut and adiposity hormones.[2] A randomized trial in gastric bypass patients compared a South Beach-based low-carbohydrate high-protein diet with a low-fat diet over 12 months.[3] An endocrinology review discussed the diet among popular low-carbohydrate approaches and insulin resistance.[5]

Reviewers have been mixed: a Harvard Health Letter said the book makes some good points but lacks proof for some claims, and a 2006 analysis of its nutrition statements assessed their support in the literature.[6][7] A 2014 systematic review cited on Wikipedia found no evidence on cardiovascular effects.[1]
A case report described a 30-year-old man who developed ketoacidosis after three weeks on the diet, having lost 16 pounds.[4] A study of menus from popular plans evaluated micronutrient adequacy.[8]

Human studies include a 12-week open study in metabolic syndrome, a randomized trial after gastric bypass, and a case report of ketoacidosis.[2][3][4] Population analysis of diet search data has estimated how long people stick to popular diets.[9]

timeline.event: Miami television segment popularizes the diet locally.[1]
The South Beach Diet book is published.[1]
